MetaSwarm at AbjadMed: Focal, Class-Balanced Optimization for Diglossic Medical Text in Abjad Scripts

Abstract

Long-tailed classification of Arabic medical text is harder than English-language priors suggest: on the AbjadMed shared task (82 classes; 27,951 train and 18,634 evaluation instances), most published systems fall between 0.35 and 0.50 macro-F1. We present MetaSwarm, a CAMeLBERT-DA system (Inoue et al., 2021) that scores 0.3588 public / 0.3520 private. Its recipe composes three standard interventions inside a five-fold, logit-mean ensemble on dual H200 GPUs: effective-number class weighting (Cui et al., 2019), focal modulation (γ=2.5) (Lin et al., 2017), and targeted oversampling of the 42 weakest classes. We contribute the full configuration, a Tail-42 audit showing that residual errors concentrate in 42 of 82 classes, and three mechanisms (dialectal shift, orthographic ambiguity, code-switching) articulated as testable hypotheses rather than asserted causes. Code, per-class counts, and seeds accompany this paper; retrieval over the training set, which the top system pairs with BERT, is the clearest remaining lever.

Method : Backbone and Loss

We fine-tune CAMeLBERT-DA (Inoue et al., 2021), a BERT variant pre-trained on dialectal Arabic: user-generated medical queries are dialectal, and an MSA-only model treats dialectal negation (mish vs. la) as noise. Two loss components address the two failure modes of imbalanced learning. Inter-class imbalance: following Cui et al. (2019), the effective number of samples E_n = (1-β^n)/(1-β) with β = 0.999 yields per-class weights

Intra-class difficulty: the focal term -α_f (1-p_t)^γ log(p_t) (Lin et al., 2017) down-weights easy examples: at γ=2, an example with p_t=0.9 contributes 1% of its cross-entropy, one with p_t=0.1 retains 81%. The submitted ensemble trains with focal cross-entropy and label smoothing ε=0.15,

with γ=2.5, α_f=0.25. The class weights of Eq. (1) were used in the development stage (and in an inverse-log-frequency variant that stabilized early single-model runs); the final ensemble uses Eq. (2). Weighting's anti-collapse effect is development evidence, not an ablated finding; the matched CE, focal-only, and weighted ablations are specified in Section 7.

Results

The ensemble scores 0.3588 public and 0.3520 private macro-F1. The 0.0068 gap sits within the ±O(0.01) split uncertainty implied by the organizers' half-and-half division of the 18,634 evaluation instances (Gupta et al., 2026), which is evidence of no public-split overfitting, though one submission cannot separate that from a ceiling effect. For calibration: the task's best systems reach 0.7422 public / 0.6732 private; among published system papers, a BERT+kNN retrieval hybrid leads at 0.4902, class-balanced AraBERT plus back-translation follows at 0.4219, and MARBERTv2 lands at 0.3659. Our score sits in the mid-band, and the leader's advantage, retrieval over the training set, is visible precisely because the field reports scores at all.

Findings

Where the errors are

Figure 3 plots per-class F1 for the baseline run against a 0.40 diagnostic line: 42 of 82 classes fall below it. The distribution is the finding: error is not spread evenly but concentrated in a tail that the macro average exists to protect. These 42 classes define the oversampling list used downstream, closing the loop between audit and intervention.

We articulate three mechanisms the tail is consistent with, and state what would decide each.

(H1) Dialectal shift. If MSA-dialect distance drives tail error, error rates should stratify by dialect markers; a dialect-annotated subsample would test this directly.

(H2) Orthographic ambiguity. Unvocalized Arabic maps one skeleton to several vocalizations; if ambiguity drives error, tokens with higher vocalization entropy should be over-represented in errors relative to their corpus frequency, a countable contrast with a significance test.

(H3) Code-switching. Patients mix Latin-script medical terms into Arabic ("3andi diabetes"); under CAMeLBERT-DA's sub-word tokenizer these fragment into short pieces. If fragmentation is the mechanism, code-switched items should show higher fragmentation rates and lower accuracy than Arabic-only items under a matched comparison, also a countable contrast. None of the three is established here; the confusion structure (Figure 4) and the attention map (Figure 5) are consistent with all three and decide none.
